title: Errors as values: wrapping with %w and adding context
summary: Errors are ordinary values you return and check. Wrap them with %w to add context without losing the cause, and inspect them later with errors.Is.

examples.title: Wrapping adds context; errors.Is still finds the cause

annotations.note: os.ReadFile already says "open users.txt" — but not who wanted it or why. Wrapping adds the loadConfig frame; it doesn't discard anything.
%w (not %v) is what makes wrapping work: it embeds the original error so errors.Is/As can unwrap. %v would only format text.

The text after the last colon comes from the operating system: "no such file or directory" on Linux and macOS, "The system cannot find the file specified." on Windows. That is why this example's check only looks at the parts Go produced.
errors.Is walks the whole chain with ==, so a sentinel like fs.ErrNotExist matches even three wrappers deep, on every OS. A string match on the message would be brittle and locale-hostile.

use_cases: Boundary functions that translate low-level errors into your domain
Adding what the operation was doing (query, file, service) without losing WHY it failed
strengths: Unlike Java checked exceptions, the compiler won't force you to handle the error — errcheck-style linters fill that role
Wrapping keeps one error chain instead of exception hierarchies; the cause and the context travel together
Sentinels like fs.ErrNotExist are comparable values: errors.Is is precise string-free matching
weaknesses: Nothing enforces checking a returned error; ignoring one is a silent bug
Deeply wrapped chains can produce noisy messages if every layer adds context
No stack trace by default: you add context deliberately instead

pitfalls.title: Wrapping with %v instead of %w
pitfalls.detail: The message looks right, but errors.Is/As can no longer see the cause. Always %w when you want unwrapping.

pitfalls.title: Checking err == fs.ErrNotExist on a wrapped error
pitfalls.detail: == only matches the immediate value. Wrapped errors must be inspected with errors.Is.

pitfalls.title: Adding context twice
pitfalls.detail: "open users.txt: open users.txt". Wrap where you add new information, not to re-log what the message already says.

quiz.q: Which verb preserves the wrapped error for errors.Is?
quiz.why: %w embeds the error value; %v and %s only format its message into the new string.

quiz.q: errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) on err = fmt.Errorf("load: %w", fmt.Errorf("open: %w", fs.ErrNotExist))?
quiz.why: errors.Is walks Unwrap() repeatedly until it finds a match or the chain ends.

body:
## Concept

A Go error is an ordinary value returned alongside your result: `value, err := doThing()`.
You check it, add context with `fmt.Errorf` and `%w`, and pass it up. `errors.Is` and
`errors.As` inspect the wrapped chain without knowing how many layers added context.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/Python/JS: exceptions unwind for you. In Go the `if err != nil` check is the unwind
  — visible, local, and impossible to trigger from a line you didn't expect to throw.
- C: errno plus return codes, but the error carries a message and an identity (`==`-able
  sentinels) instead of a global mutable code.
- Rust: `Result<T, E>` with `?` ≈ `(T, error)` with `if err != nil`; Go's `return err` is
  the explicit version of `?`.

## Design notes

Add context at each layer that knows something new ("loading config", "querying orders for
user 42"), and let `errors.Is`/`As` answer inspection questions at the top. Handle the error
once: either respond to it meaningfully or wrap and pass it up — logging it *and* returning
it produces duplicate log lines for one failure. This lesson's strategy across layers
(sentinel vs typed errors, where to recover) is its own later lesson.

expected.wrap:
load config: open users.txt:
not exist? true
